activities.caption: fill the blanks — the GDP definition
activities.name: gdpDefCloze

config.text: GDP is the market value of all %%0%% goods and services produced in a country in a year. It is built from four spending streams: %%1%% + I + G + NX, where NX means %%2%%.
config.hint: Only final goods count, and the four buckets are consumption, investment, government and net exports.

activities.anchor: Every transaction in an economy has two sides
activities.caption: value added down the bread chain
activities.name: gdpLoafOrder

config.prompt: A farmer, a miller and a baker make one loaf economy — put the value-added accounting in order:
items: The farmer produces grain and sells it for £100 (value added £100)
The miller buys the grain for £100 and sells flour for £150 (value added £50)
The baker buys the flour for £150 and sells bread for £260 (value added £110)
The same £260 appears as household expenditure on the final bread
config.why: Each stage's value added is its output minus its intermediate inputs. Summing those gaps and summing final expenditure are the same arithmetic run in opposite directions.

activities.anchor: household spending on goods and services
activities.caption: counts in GDP, or not?
activities.name: gdpCountSort

config.prompt: Which of these enter this year's GDP?

items.label: a new factory built this year
buying shares of an existing company
a pension payment from the state
a haircut bought at a salon
the full resale price of a 2018 car

config.why: Only new final production counts. Share purchases transfer existing assets, pensions are transfers, unpaid work is invisible, and a resale adds only the dealer's margin.

activities.anchor: The readouts show typical rich-country shares
activities.caption: true or false — reading the four buckets
activities.name: gdpBucketJudge

statements.s: Consumption is typically 60–70% of GDP in rich economies.
statements.why: Household spending is the giant bucket, which is why consumer confidence is macroeconomic news.

statements.s: Buying shares counts as investment in the national accounts.
statements.why: Investment means new productive capacity — machines, factories, software, housing, inventories — not the transfer of existing assets.

statements.s: Transfer payments such as pensions are part of government spending G.
statements.why: They are excluded from G because they buy no output; their spending enters C when recipients spend them.

activities.anchor: Four adjustments convert the raw total
activities.caption: call the real growth rate
activities.name: gdpRealEst

config.prompt: Nominal GDP rose 6% while the price level rose 4%. What was real growth?
config.why: Real growth strips out inflation: about 6% − 4% = 2%. The GDP deflator is the conversion factor (nominal ÷ real × 100).
config.context: every growth claim worth quoting is a real figure

activities.caption: production versus welfare — drag the divider
activities.name: gdpWelfareCompare

config.prompt: One number, two questions — drag the divider:

before.label: GDP
before.text: the market value of final output — built to track production through recessions, not to score a society

after.label: welfare dashboard
after.text: health, education, distribution, unpaid work and environmental depletion — what GDP leaves out

config.why: Kuznets warned in 1934 that national income cannot measure a nation's welfare; the dashboard tries to count what the production total omits.

activities.anchor: Real GDP's movements are the economy's vital signs
activities.caption: mark the doubling time at 2% growth
activities.name: gdpDoublePlace

config.prompt: At 2% annual real growth, roughly how many years until output doubles? Place it on the axis.
config.why: The rule of 70 gives 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years. Compounding turns a small growth rate into a large change in living standards.

activities.anchor: the US also uses the NBER's broader judgment
activities.caption: is it a recession?
activities.name: gdpRecessionBranch

config.root: Real GDP falls for two consecutive quarters, then grows in the third. Trace the diagnosis.

start.text: Using the conventional rule, what is this?

choices.label: A recession — two consecutive quarterly falls
choices.feedback: Yes — the two falls meet the conventional threshold.

choices.label: Not a recession, because the third quarter grew
choices.feedback: The rule looks at the two consecutive falls; the later recovery does not erase them.

choices.label: A depression
choices.feedback: Depression is an informal, deeper and longer event; two quarters is the recession threshold.

rule.text: The conventional rule is two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP. The US also uses the NBER's broader judgment — income, employment, sales and production, not GDP alone.

grew.text: The third quarter's growth marks the recovery, not the absence of the recession.

depression.text: A depression is an informal label for a deeper, longer downturn; the conventional recession threshold is two quarters.

config.why: The two-quarter rule is a convention; the NBER's broader dating uses income, employment, sales and production because GDP alone can mislead.

activities.anchor: The three routes agree by construction, but
activities.caption: find the double-counted loaf
activities.name: gdpLoafSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the value-added arithmetic goes wrong:
lines: The farmer sells £100 of grain to the miller.
The miller sells £150 of flour to the baker.
The baker sells £260 of bread to households.
config.correction: Value added at each stage is £100, £50 and £110 — the £150 flour price and £260 bread price are not themselves value added.
config.why: Adding each stage's full selling price double-counts the intermediate goods already embodied in the final bread.

activities.caption: pair each alternative with what it adds
activities.name: gdpAlternativesMatch

config.prompt: Pair each alternative measure with what it adds to GDP:

pairs.right: averages income, life expectancy and schooling
Bhutan's dashboard of life satisfaction and environment

config.why: Each alternative encodes a philosophy of what matters — and each is also an index-number choice with weighting politics.
